sections.report:
I've checked the "whole piece" section. 6 of its 8 lines pass and 2 fail, and both failures come from one hero image that doesn't match its headline.

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **"Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?"** and **"Do the colors, shapes, and directions of the piece carry the mood its message calls for?"** (one problem, two `no` lines)
   - **Where:** the full-width hero, rows 60–460 px, behind "Plants for shade and small spaces" at about x 70–665, y 205–310.
   - **What the viewer gets:** the picture is a dense, bright pattern of foliage. It has light yellow-green and sunny yellow leaves, orange and red berries, and white dots, all evenly lit with no shadow. Nothing in it says shade, and nothing says small space: there's no pot, no balcony and no tight corner. So the image only repeats the word "plants". The page's actual offer, plants that thrive where light and room are short, falls entirely on the headline. The image's mood also runs against that offer: it reads as summer sun, not cool, dappled shade.
   - **Cost:** the visitor this page is for has a dim yard or a small balcony. The hero doesn't show them their own situation, so it doesn't tell them "this is for you". It looks like generic garden-centre stock. The busy pattern also runs straight through the headline: in the 50,190 crop, pale leaves cross "shade", "small" and the "s" of "spaces". The text and colour critics will cover legibility, but the cause is the same choice of image.
   - **Why:** colour temperature, saturation and value should support the message and not contradict the subject (Itten, *The Art of Color*). The image-and-headline point has no approved source, so it is argued here as common sense.
   - **Fix:** choose or redraw the hero so it shows the promise itself. That could be deep, cool greens with low, dappled light, ferns and hostas, or plants in a pot or a narrow corner, so picture and headline make one idea. At the same time, give the headline a calm, darker area to sit on.
   - **Kind and weight:** defect, with a convention (Itten) for the colour mood. Major.

**What's working.**
- **The three cards (y 564–678):** "Opening hours", "Saturday workshops" and "Delivery" each name exactly what's inside. Each card answers a real visitor question with specifics: hours plus the Thursday exception, ten places per class, free delivery within ten miles over $60. The copy is finished and concrete, not filler.
- **The header:** the dark-green serif wordmark sits with plain sans-serif navigation and body text. It reads as one restrained, local-business voice rather than a collage.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (main image and headline make one idea; colours carry the mood the message calls for)

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does one element stand clearly above the rest, by size or by contrast, so the eye knows where to start?** No. The headline "Plants for shade and small spaces" (about 48 px bold white, x 72–660, y 210–305) is the biggest type on the page. But it sits straight on the leaf illustration (y 60–460), and that illustration is the loudest thing on screen: full width, dense, high in contrast, and spotted with red and yellow dots. The white letters land on pale yellow and light-green leaves, so their edges dissolve, most of all through "small" and "spaces" in the crop. The eye goes to the pattern first and then has to look for the headline, so the headline and the picture compete for first place. The headline was clearly meant to lead (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*: one dominant element the eye reaches first; Tschichold, *The New Typography*: logical order shown by difference). Fix: make the headline clearly first by quieting what is behind it, not by making it bigger. You could put a solid or dark scrim panel behind the text block, darken or blur the left part of the illustration, or move the headline onto plain ground and let the picture be the picture. **Defect. Weight: major.** It's the first thing every visitor meets, and it sets whether the page reads in a clear order.

**What's working.**
- The levels below the hero are well separated. The intro line (~19 px regular), the card titles (~17 px bold) and the card text (~15 px regular) each have an obvious job. Weight, not another size, separates title from body (Refactoring UI: bolder, not bigger), so the three cards scan as title then detail without effort.
- The three cards have equal weight on purpose. Hours, workshops and delivery are peers, and treating them as a matched set is right. It avoids a fake ranking among them.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (one element dominates).

sections.report:
I've finished the walk. I'm sending the arrangement report now.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do all blocks, pictures included, take their edges and the gaps between them from one grid? / Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?** The logo, the intro line ("Ferns, hostas…") and the left card all share a left edge at x≈56. The hero headline starts at x≈72, about 16 px further in. That's too small a gap to read as a choice, so it looks like the headline was placed by eye. The page's one strong vertical line breaks at its most important element, and the hero looks slightly loose next to the tidy band below. Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I: a placement that is almost aligned makes the eye waver. Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems*: every block takes its edges from one grid. **Fix:** move the headline onto the x≈56 line. If it is meant to sit inside a padded hero, give it a clear inset that the content below repeats. Convention. Weight: minor.
2. **Does each card, panel, tint, or border hold exactly one group, with no group split across boxes?** The hero's message is split in two. The headline sits inside the leaf image (y≈210–310), but the line that explains it sits on white below the image edge (y≈485–535). The hard edge at y≈460 cuts the headline from its own supporting line. The intro line ends up looking like the start of the lower content instead of the second half of the hero statement, and the headline is left alone in the pattern. Palmer 1992 / Nielsen Norman Group, "Common Region". **Fix:** put the headline and intro line in one region. Either move both onto a calm area or panel inside the hero, or move the headline down onto the white so it sits right above the intro line, with the picture as a band above them. Defect. Weight: major.
3. **Does each element stay clear of the others, with no text or box overlapping or touching another?** The headline is set straight on top of the dense leaf illustration, with nothing behind the type. Pale yellow and light-green leaves run through and touch the letters, especially "small" (x≈540–660) and "spaces" (x≈72–235). The text and the picture compete in the same spot, so the type is hard to pick out. The catalog has no entry for this, so it's my judgment (common sense). The contrast side belongs to the colour and text sections. **Fix:** give the headline a quiet field. Use a solid or scrim panel, clear a calm area in the illustration behind the type, or take the type off the picture (see finding 2). Taste / common sense. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- The lower band follows one clear structure. The three cards are equal width with equal ~28 px gutters, their outer edges match the margins of the logo and the nav (x≈56 and x≈1224), and their headings and body lines sit on shared baselines. As a result, the three facts read as one set at a glance.
- The proportions are simple and clear: the hero takes half the frame (y≈60–460 of 800) and the cards split the width into thirds. The open area to the right of the intro line gives the eye somewhere to rest before the cards.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** There is an empty band about 120 px tall under the cards (y≈680–800). It may simply be where the capture ends, or the page may stop there. Check a live browser to see whether more content follows. If none does, the page ends on dead space.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 9 yes, 4 no (one grid; exact alignment, no near-misses; one group per box; elements clear of each other)

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does text over a photo, gradient, or texture stay readable at the worst point behind it? No.** The hero headline "Plants for shade and small spaces" (about x 72–660, y 210–310) is white bold sans set straight onto the leaf illustration, with no scrim, shadow or panel. Pale yellow and lime leaves pass right behind the letters: behind "small" (around x 540–660, y 215–255), behind "spaces" (x 72–235, y 265–310), and the white dots near x 238, y 300. In those spots the letters blend into the leaves, so the end of the page's main promise breaks up and takes a second look to read. That is the line that tells a visitor what this nursery is offering right now. Where the leaves are dark green it reads fine, but contrast has to hold at the worst point behind the text, not on average (W3C, Techniques for WCAG 2.2, F83, under SC 1.4.3). Fix: put a dark scrim, a see-through overlay, or a solid panel behind the text, or move the text to a calm part of the image, so that every letter stands out from what is directly behind it. A darkened left third of the hero, or a quieter, darker leaf field behind the headline, would do it. **Defect. Weight: major.**

2. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries, never between a number and its unit or inside a name? No.** There are two breaks:
   - **Hero headline:** it breaks "small / spaces" (y ≈ 233 / 287), splitting the phrase "small spaces" and leaving "spaces" alone on line 2. The viewer reads "Plants for shade and small" as a complete thought, then has to rejoin it. Breaking after "shade" ("Plants for shade / and small spaces") keeps each phrase whole and balances the two lines. In a responsive layout, a non-breaking space or a narrower max width gets there.
   - **Opening hours card:** it reads "until 8 / pm on Thursdays" (x 80–378, y 625–647), splitting a time from its unit. The late opening is the one thing in that card a visitor acts on, and the break makes it read as "8" plus a stray "pm". A non-breaking space in "8 pm" (and "6 pm") fixes it.

   Common sense; the catalog entry was not opened because the entries script was unavailable. **Defect** for the card (it is a time the reader acts on), **taste** for the headline. **Weight: minor.**

**What's working.**
- **Typeface plan.** The serif logotype "Fernhollow Garden Center" and the plain sans used for everything else are clearly different faces with clearly different jobs. The serif gives the brand a crafted, nursery-sign feel, and the sans keeps the practical copy plain. They don't fight.
- **Intro line and card text.** The intro at about 18 px is set flush left with about 60–65 characters per line and comfortable leading. The card text is bold title over regular body at a readable size and good contrast on white, which suits glanceable facts like hours, workshops and delivery.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** How the headline wraps at other viewport widths. Both the "small / spaces" break and the leaves behind each word will shift, so check readability over the illustration at mobile and wide desktop widths. Bash was refused, so I couldn't zoom in to check fine spacing. I judged the headline's letter spacing and kerning at full size only, where it looks acceptable.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 28 yes, 2 no (text over a photo or texture readable at the worst point; headings and captions break at phrase boundaries)

sections.report:
Walk (color section, whole image ~1280×800, no crop needed; crop script unavailable because Bash was refused):
- Small palette: yes (greens/yellow from the illustration, a dark-green logo, neutral grays; red and orange appear only as illustration accents)
- Saturated color kept to a small share: no. The hero band (y 60–460, full width, about half the screen) is solid, vivid green and yellow.
- Value range / grayscale structure: no. The white headline's value matches the pale-yellow leaves and white dots behind it.
- Warm forward / cool back: no. Warm yellow leaves and red/orange dots sit in the background layer and come forward. The focal headline is neutral white.
- Matching colors consistent: yes
- No vibrating edges: no. Small red dots sit on mid-green leaves at about the same lightness.
- Status colors: yes (the red reads as berries, not as an error)
- Color not alone for meaning: yes
- Dark theme: yes (not a dark theme)

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the piece hold a clear range of light and dark, so its structure still shows in grayscale?** (also covers *Is strong, saturated color kept to a small share of the area…?* and *Do warm colors sit on what should come forward and cool ones on what should recede?*)
   - **Where:** the hero band, full width, y ≈ 60–460, and the headline at x ≈ 70–665, y ≈ 205–310.
   - **What the viewer sees:** the most saturated, highest-contrast area on the page is the backdrop, not the message. The headline is white. Behind it are pale-yellow and pale-green leaves, white dots (for example at x ≈ 237, y ≈ 300) and warm yellow and orange shapes. In grayscale, the letters of "shade and small" and "spaces" blend into the light leaves. The warm yellows and red dots advance, so the background pulls forward while the neutral headline sinks into it. The eye sees foliage first and has to work to read the one line that says what the page offers.
   - **Why:** value carries figure and ground (Albers, *Interaction of Color*; Wathan and Schoger, *Refactoring UI*). Warm colors advance and cool colors recede (Itten, *The Art of Color*). A large area of fully saturated color weakens emphasis (Itten, contrast of saturation; *Refactoring UI*).
   - **Fix:** push the band toward one value so the headline has clear value separation from everything behind it. One way is to darken the illustration behind the text with a dark green scrim, or mute or dark-shade the whole band and drop the pale and warm leaves from the text zone. The other is to place the headline on a solid panel. Keep full-strength yellow and red for small accents away from the type.
   - **Type and weight:** defect, major.
   - **Note for the director:** the legibility side of this is also a text-over-image contrast failure (WCAG F83), which the Text critic will likely file.
2. **Do neighboring strong colors differ clearly in lightness, so no edge between them seems to vibrate?**
   - **Where:** the small red dots scattered across the hero, for example at x ≈ 802, y ≈ 85; x ≈ 479, y ≈ 113; x ≈ 956, y ≈ 184; x ≈ 636, y ≈ 407.
   - **What the viewer sees:** these red dots sit directly on mid-green leaves of about the same lightness. Red on green at equal value makes their edges shimmer and adds more visual noise to an already busy band. For red-green color-blind viewers the dots disappear into the leaves, which is harmless here because they carry no meaning.
   - **Why:** Albers, *Interaction of Color*; Itten, *The Art of Color*.
   - **Fix:** make the red clearly darker or lighter than the greens it touches, mute it, or give the dots a pale gap around them.
   - **Type and weight:** convention, minor.

**What's working.**
- **The palette is tight and on-subject.** One green-yellow family, plus a red accent that reads as berries, with a matching dark green for the "Fernhollow Garden Center" logo. The brand color and the illustration feel like one system, and the palette fits a garden center.
- **Below the hero, color stays out of the way.** The intro line, the three cards and the nav are neutral: white surfaces, near-black type and light-gray borders. All the color is in one place, and the practical information reads calmly.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 6 yes, 3 no (strong color kept to a small share; clear value range in grayscale; warm forward, cool back) — the vibrating-edges line is also no, so the final tally is 9 lines, 5 yes, 4 no (strong color kept to a small share; clear value range in grayscale; warm forward, cool back; no vibrating edges).

sections.report:
**Section.** Pictures: applies. There is one illustration (the leaf pattern in the hero, about 0–1280 × 60–460 px) and one wordmark logo. Bash was blocked, so I couldn't make crops and judged everything from the full image at 1280×800.

**Findings**
1. **Is any texture or pattern quiet enough that it never competes with the focal point or the text over it? No.**
   - **Where:** The white headline "Plants for shade and small spaces" sits at about x 72–660, y 205–310, directly on the leaf pattern.
   - **What the viewer gets:** The pattern is busy and high-contrast all the way across. Pale yellow and lime leaves, white dots and red berries sit next to dark green, and none of it is dimmed or softened behind the type. Where pale leaves cross the letters, the white type has almost no contrast. This happens around "small", the "s" of "spaces" and the descenders. The letters break up into the leaves, so the eye lands on the pattern first and has to work to read the headline. The headline is the page's main message, so this costs the page its first read.
   - **Why:** This is common sense; the catalog entry ("Texture and pattern with restraint") has no approved source. Pattern behind text should be limited in area or low in contrast so it doesn't hurt legibility. It also overlaps the Color section's question about text over a busy image, so the director should file it in one place.
   - **Fix:** Calm the area behind the headline. Options are a dark green scrim or gradient over the left side, a lower-contrast version of the pattern there, a solid panel behind the type, or moving the headline off the pattern into the white band below. Check contrast against the palest leaf, not the average.
   - **Type and weight:** Defect. Major.

2. **Off the checklist: the picture doesn't show the offer.**
   - **Where:** The whole hero.
   - **What the viewer gets:** The headline and intro promise ferns, hostas and compact shrubs for shade. The illustration is generic leaves in bright, sunlit yellow-greens. It reads as "garden centre" in general rather than shade plants. Nothing in it is recognisably a fern or a hosta, and the mood is sunny rather than shaded.
   - **Why it matters:** The hero takes half the screen but adds no information. A visitor can't recognise the plants on offer and isn't shown what makes this nursery different.
   - **Fix:** Use a picture that shows the real subject. That could be a photo of their own ferns and hostas in a shady corner or on a balcony, or an illustration with recognisable fern fronds and hosta leaves in a cooler, deeper palette.
   - **Type and weight:** Taste. Minor if the overlay fix is done; it becomes more important if the hero is meant to sell.

**What's working.**
- **The leaf illustration is well made.** It is crisp flat vector with one consistent rendering style and level of detail, and its greens are clearly related to the dark green of the wordmark. The hero and the brand belong together.
- **The wordmark is right for a small business.** "Fernhollow Garden Center" (about x 56–342, y 18–40) is a plain serif in one dark green with generous space around it. It stays readable at small sizes and in one colour.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 11 yes, 1 no (pattern quiet enough not to compete with the text over it).

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye lands on the white headline over the leaf pattern, then moves to the three cards. It reads as a local garden centre's home page and feels friendly and calm. The only things that look clickable are the four grey nav links at the top right. Nothing in the page body offers a next step.

Job (assumed): a garden centre's home page for local shoppers. It should get them to browse plants, book a workshop, or plan a visit.

Image is about 1280×800, one screen, so no crops were needed. Bash is refused in this session, so I could not run the crop or entries scripts and judged from the whole image.

Interface:
- Exactly one primary button, others lower: **no**. The page has no button at all.
- Controls look like what they do: **no**. The three cards (56–1224, 564–678) have a border and rounded corners like clickable tiles, but nothing says whether they are links.
- 3:1 contrast on control edges: yes (the nav is text; the card borders count only if the cards are controls, which is covered under the line above).
- States shown: yes (none shown).
- Focus indicator / focus not obscured: unsure, can't tell from a still.
- Main content uncovered: yes.
- Target sizes: yes (nav links look about 16 px tall plus padding, about 28 px apart).
- Phone thumb zone: yes (not a phone layout).
- Shows where the user is: yes (home page; no active nav item is normal).
- Way out / valid inputs / destructive set apart: yes (none present).
- Recognition over recall: yes.
- Progressive disclosure: yes.
- Form lines (labels, single column, required, errors, error fixes): yes (no form).
- Empty states / help / shortcuts: yes (not needed here).
- Anticipation: yes. Hours and delivery terms are already on the page.
- Conventions: yes (logo left, nav right).
- Audience's words: yes.
- Link purpose: yes.
- Sensory instructions: yes.
- Conceptual model: yes.
- Consistency across screens: yes (only one screen).
- Reflow: yes.
- Honest choices: yes.

---

**Section.** Interface: applies (top nav links; the cards may be interactive).

**Findings**
1. **Is exactly one button styled as the primary action, with every other action styled lower?** No. The page has no button or call to action anywhere. Under the hero, the lede (56–700, 485–540) promises "Ferns, hostas and compact shrubs… ready to pot this weekend", and nothing below it lets you act on that. The "Saturday workshops" card says "ten places in each class", which makes you want to book, but you can't. The only routes forward are four small grey nav links at the top right (948–1224, y≈28). A visitor who is sold by the headline has to go back up and guess that "Plants" leads to these shade plants. Defect: the page builds intent and then gives it nowhere to go. Fix direction: add one clearly styled primary button tied to the headline's offer, such as "Shop shade plants", just under the lede. Give the other actions lower styling, as text links inside the cards: "Book a workshop" and "Delivery details". Weight: **major**.
2. **Does every control look like what it does, buttons pressable, fields typeable, and links marked by more than color?** No. The three cards (each about 370×114 px, at y 564–678) are drawn as bordered, rounded tiles, a shape that usually means "click me". They have no arrow, link text, or heading styling to confirm it. Either they are links that don't look like links, or they are static boxes that look like links. Either way the visitor has to try them to find out (Norman, signifiers). If they are clickable, their pale grey border also looks well under 3:1 against white, so the text is the only thing marking the target. Defect, small. Fix direction: if the cards link somewhere, add a visible link line or arrow to each ("See times →"). If they don't, drop the border-and-radius tile look so they read as plain information blocks. Weight: **minor**.

**What's working.**
- The nav follows the convention visitors expect (wordmark left, four short links right). Its labels are in shoppers' own words ("Plants", "Workshops", "Visit"), so it is easy to scan.
- The page answers the practical questions up front: opening hours, workshop format, and the delivery threshold of $60 within ten miles. A visitor doesn't have to dig for them.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether the nav links and cards show a visible focus indicator, and whether they change on hover. This matters because the nav is currently the page's only way forward.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 29 yes, 2 no (one primary action; controls look like what they do), 2 unsure (focus indicator; focus not obscured).

Bash was refused in this session, so I couldn't run the crop or entries scripts. I judged from the full image, which is one screen and needed no crops, and I didn't open the reference entries for the two "no" lines.
